stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of permanent atrial fibrillation comes to the office for follow-up. He has been having symptoms due to ineffective ventricular rate control despite aggressive medical therapy. On examination, the patient's heart rate is 125/min and irregular. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. A catheter-based radiofrequency ablation of the atrioventricular node with placement of a permanent ventricular pacemaker is planned. The ablation tip should be positioned at which of the following locations?

options.A: Between the tricuspid valve and the inferior vena cava opening
options.B: Interatrial septum near the opening of the coronary sinus
options.C: Left atrium near the opening of the pulmonary veins
options.D: The posterior border of the fossa ovalis
options.E: Upper part of crista terminalis near the superior vena cava opening

explanations.A: The isthmus between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus is the site of radiofrequency ablation for atrial flutter. The fossa ovalis is the name given to the foramen ovale once it is closed. However, neither option refers to the location of the AV node.
explanations.B: The AV node is located on the endocardial surface of the right atrium, near the insertion of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and the orifice of the coronary sinus.
explanations.C: The pulmonary vein ostia are often the origination site of the aberrant electrical activity that triggers atrial fibrillation, and catheter ablation of these trigger sites (pulmonary vein isolation) can be used to prevent recurrent atrial fibrillation. However, this patient has already developed permanent atrial fibrillation and is undergoing an ablation procedure involving the AV node.
explanations.D: The fossa ovalis is the closed remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, not the location of the AV node.
explanations.E: The sinoatrial node is located in the upper anterior right atrium at the opening of the superior vena cava.

generalExplanation: The atrioventricular (AV) node controls the rate at which atrial impulses are conducted to the ventricles. In patients with atrial fibrillation, continuous stimulation of the AV node can sometimes lead to a rapid ventricular rate, which can cause hemodynamic instability and (if persistent) tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. In order to prevent these complications, patients with a rapid ventricular response sometimes undergo radiofrequency ablation of the AV node. The AV node is located on the endocardial surface of the right atrium, near the insertion of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and the orifice of the coronary sinus.
educationalObjective: The atrioventricular node is located on the endocardial surface of the right atrium, near the insertion of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and the orifice of the coronary sinus.

stem: A 20-year-old, previously healthy woman is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. The patient was a restrained, rear-seat passenger when another car struck the side door. There was extensive damage to the vehicle, resulting in a prolonged extrication time. On arrival at the emergency department, blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg and pulse is 120/min. On physical examination, the patient is alert but appears anxious, pale, and diaphoretic. There is no obvious head or neck injury. The lungs are clear bilaterally and cardiac auscultation reveals tachycardia. The abdomen is soft. Several actively bleeding lacerations are present on the lower extremities. X-rays show pelvic and left femoral shaft fractures. Which of the following findings are most likely present in this patient?

options.A: Cardiac contractility: ↑ | Baroreceptor firing: ↑ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↑
options.B: Cardiac contractility: ↓ | Baroreceptor firing: ↑ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↑
options.C: Cardiac contractility: ↑ | Baroreceptor firing: ↓ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↑
options.D: Cardiac contractility: ↓ | Baroreceptor firing: ↑ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↓
options.E: Cardiac contractility: ↑ | Baroreceptor firing: ↓ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↓
options.F: Cardiac contractility: ↓ | Baroreceptor firing: ↓ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↓
options.G: Cardiac contractility: ↓ | Baroreceptor firing: ↓ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↑
options.H: Cardiac contractility: ↑ | Baroreceptor firing: ↑ | Atrial natriuretic peptide release: ↓

explanations.A: Because baroreceptor firing reduces sympathetic output, the degree of baroreceptor firing is usually inversely related to cardiac contractility.
explanations.B: In hypervolemic states, blood pressure is increased, leading to increased baroreceptor firing with a decrease in sympathetic outflow and corresponding increase in parasympathetic outflow. Increased stretching of the atrial walls leads to increased ANP release.
explanations.C: Because conditions that increase or decrease baroreceptor stretch typically have the same effect on atrial stretch, the degree of baroreceptor firing is usually directly related to the level of ANP release.
explanations.D: Low blood volume reduces both baroreceptor firing and atrial stretch (ANP release).
explanations.E: Reduced stretch of the arterial walls leads to reduced baroreceptor firing, increasing sympathetic outflow and contractility. Hypovolemia also reduces atrial stretch, decreasing ANP release.
explanations.F: Sympathetic activation increases cardiac contractility rather than decreasing it.
explanations.G: Hypovolemia decreases ANP release and increases contractility.
explanations.H: Baroreceptor firing is decreased due to low blood pressure and reduced arterial wall stretch.

generalExplanation: This patient's hypotension and tachycardia in the setting of multiple lacerations and pelvic fracture are consistent with hypovolemic shock due to massive hemorrhage. Following significant intravascular volume depletion, baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries rapidly adjust autonomic output to help maintain blood pressure. Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors that increase their firing rate in response to arterial distension. With an abrupt decrease in cardiac output and blood pressure, reduced stretch of the arterial walls leads to reduced baroreceptor firing and decreased activation of the solitary nucleus. This causes an increase in sympathetic outflow with a corresponding reduction in parasympathetic tone, leading to vasoconstriction and increased heart rate and contractility. Via a similar mechanism, stretch receptors in the atrial walls control secretion of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). With hypovolemia there is reduced atrial stretch that leads to decreased ANP secretion.
educationalObjective: Low blood pressure results in decreased arterial distension and reduced firing of aortic and carotid baroreceptors. This leads to an increase in sympathetic outflow and decrease in parasympathetic outflow, stimulating vasoconstriction and increased heart rate and contractility in order to help maintain blood pressure. Hypovolemia reduces atrial stretch, causing decreased atrial natriuretic peptide secretion.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is being evaluated for fatigue and progressive exertional dyspnea. She goes mountain biking with friends a few times a month and recently noticed that she has to stop and rest more frequently when traveling uphill. The patient has no significant medical history and takes no medications. She occasionally drinks alcohol but does not use tobacco or illicit drugs. Her father died of a myocardial infarction at age 72. Lung auscultation is normal. An echocardiogram shows an enlarged coronary sinus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the observed finding in this patient?

explanations.A: Aortic dissection can occur in patients with severe hypertension. Such patients might have elevated left heart pressures, but elevated right-sided heart pressures with dilation of the CS would be unlikely.
explanations.B: The presence of asymptomatic coronary artery disease usually does not change the size of the CS. Long-standing left ventricular systolic dysfunction due to prior myocardial infarction can lead to secondary pulmonary hypertension, with the possibility of CS dilation over time.
explanations.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy usually manifests as asymmetric septal hypertrophy. CS dilation should not occur unless there is superimposed biventricular heart failure.
explanations.D: Pericardial effusion can cause extrinsic compression of the coronary sinus rather than dilation.
explanations.E: The coronary sinus communicates freely with the right atrium and will become dilated secondary to any factor that causes increased right atrial pressure. The most common cause is pulmonary hypertension, leading to elevated right heart pressures.

generalExplanation: Most of the venous drainage from the myocardium traverses the coronary sinus (CS), which delivers deoxygenated blood to the right atrium. The CS runs transversely in the left atrioventricular groove on the posterior aspect of the heart, and opens into the right atrium between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid valve at the CS orifice. Because the CS communicates freely with the right atrium, it will become dilated by any factor that causes dilation of the right atrium. The most common cause of coronary sinus dilation evident on echocardiography is elevated right-sided heart pressure secondary to pulmonary hypertension. CS dilation also occurs in patients with anomalous venous drainage into the CS, including persistent left superior vena cava and total anomalous pulmonary venous return.
educationalObjective: The coronary sinus communicates freely with the right atrium and will become dilated secondary to any factor that causes increased right atrial pressure. The most common cause is pulmonary hypertension, leading to elevated right heart pressures.

stem: A 53-year-old man comes to the office due to difficulty breathing and increasing fatigue. He has shortness of breath at night and has been sleeping in a recliner to help relieve his dyspnea. Medical history is significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Two months ago, the patient suffered a myocardial infarction that was not revascularized due to a delay in seeking treatment. He quit smoking afterward, but had previously smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. On cardiac auscultation, a low-frequency diastolic heart sound is heard shortly after the second heart sound when the patient lies in the left lateral decubitus position. Cardiac imaging shows hypokinesis of the left ventricular free wall. Which of the following is most likely to accentuate this patient's abnormal auscultation finding?

explanations.A: Amyl nitrite inhalation causes vasodilation, resulting in a transient decrease in venous return and blood pressure. It would lessen S3 intensity due to the reduction in end-systolic ventricular volume.
explanations.B: Furosemide injection would lead to brisk diuresis, resulting in a decrease in end-systolic ventricular volume that would likely lessen S3 intensity.
explanations.C: Abrupt standing decreases venous return to the heart and ventricular volumes, reducing S3 intensity.
explanations.D: Listening at end expiration makes the sound even more audible by decreasing lung volume and bringing the heart closer to the chest wall.
explanations.E: The straining phase (phase 2) of the Valsalva maneuver decreases venous return to the heart and reduces S3 intensity.

generalExplanation: This patient has decompensated heart failure with an audible third heart sound (S3), a low-frequency sound that occurs shortly after S2 during diastole. S3 is caused by a sudden limitation of ventricular movement during rapid passive ventricular filling. It can be a normal finding in healthy children and young adults. However, the presence of S3 in patients age >40 is considered abnormal and suggests ventricular volume overload or enlargement. It is often heard with aortic/mitral regurgitation or systolic heart failure. Left ventricular gallops (S3 and/or S4) are best heard with the bell of the stethoscope over the cardiac apex while the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. Listening at end expiration makes the sound even more audible by decreasing lung volume and bringing the heart closer to the chest wall.
educationalObjective: The third heart sound (S3) is a low-frequency sound occurring during early diastole after S2. Left ventricular gallops (S3 and/or S4) are best heard with the bell of the stethoscope over the cardiac apex while the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position at end expiration.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office due to exertional dyspnea. The patient has a history of IgA nephropathy; she received hemodialysis for 2 years before undergoing kidney transplantation last month. Chest x-ray reveals cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion. Further evaluation determines that her symptoms are likely due to persistence of the arteriovenous fistula that was used for hemodialysis. Which of the following physiologic changes are most likely present in this patient due to the fistula?

options.A: Cardiac output: ↓ | Systemic vascular resistance: ↑ | Venous return: ↓
options.B: Cardiac output: ↓ | Systemic vascular resistance: ↑ | Venous return: ↑
options.C: Cardiac output: ↑ | Systemic vascular resistance: ↓ | Venous return: ↓
options.D: Cardiac output: ↑ | Systemic vascular resistance: ↓ | Venous return: ↑
options.E: Cardiac output: ↑ | Systemic vascular resistance: ↑ | Venous return: ↑

explanations.A: Hypovolemia involves a marked reduction in blood volume with decreased venous return, reduced cardiac output, and a compensatory increase in SVR.
explanations.B: Low-output heart failure involves left ventricular dysfunction leading to decreased cardiac output and compensatory increase in SVR.
explanations.C: In sepsis, reduced SVR occurs with compensatory increase in cardiac output, but leaky vasculature reduces intravascular volume and venous return.
explanations.D: A large arteriovenous fistula allows blood flow to bypass systemic arteriolar resistance, causing markedly decreased SVR. Low peripheral resistance increases venous return, which together with reduced afterload markedly increases cardiac output.
explanations.E: Arteriolar and venoconstriction from alpha-1 stimulation increases SVR and venous return, but an AV fistula lowers SVR.

generalExplanation: This patient with dyspnea and chest x-ray showing an enlarged heart and pulmonary edema likely has high-output heart failure due to excessive flow through her arteriovenous fistula. A large arteriovenous fistula allows a high proportion of blood flow to bypass the resistance of the systemic arterioles, causing markedly decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR) (reduced afterload). Blood passing through the low peripheral resistance returns to the right atrium quickly and easily, resulting in increased venous return (increased preload). Both the reduced afterload and increased preload facilitate increased stroke volume and cardiac output. With excessively large fistulas, the left ventricle becomes unable to keep up with the increased venous return despite a persistent increase in cardiac output; left ventricular diastolic pressure gradually increases, and decompensated heart failure develops.
educationalObjective: High-output heart failure results from markedly decreased systemic vascular resistance (eg, large arteriovenous fistula) that leads to increased venous return and increased cardiac output. Despite a sustained increase in cardiac output, the left ventricle is unable to keep up with the increased venous return, and decompensated heart failure develops.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the clinic for a routine physical. The patient has no medical problems and takes no medication. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. He plays on his college football team and participates in intense training sessions and weekly games. Review of systems is unremarkable. Blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg, pulse is 68/min, and respirations are 15/min. BMI is 28 kg/m². Blood pressures in the upper and lower extremities are equal. There is no jugular venous distension. Carotid upstrokes are brisk. There is a grade 2/6 early systolic murmur along the left sternal border. The murmur decreases in intensity with hand grip and passive leg elevation. Lung sounds are normal without crackles or wheezes. Echocardiogram is most likely to demonstrate which of the following findings?

options.A: LV mass: Increased | LV cavity size: Dilated | LV ejection fraction: Decreased | LV relaxation: Normal
options.B: LV mass: Increased | LV cavity size: Normal | LV ejection fraction: Preserved | LV relaxation: Normal
options.C: LV mass: Increased | LV cavity size: Small | LV ejection fraction: Decreased | LV relaxation: Impaired
options.D: LV mass: Increased | LV cavity size: Small | LV ejection fraction: Preserved | LV relaxation: Impaired
options.E: LV mass: Normal | LV cavity size: Normal | LV ejection fraction: Preserved | LV relaxation: Impaired

explanations.A: Increased LV mass with a dilated LV cavity, decreased LV ejection fraction, and normal LV relaxation are consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy.
explanations.B: Increased LV mass with normal LV relaxation and normal LV cavity size and ejection fraction are consistent with athlete's heart, which lacks an HCM murmur.
explanations.C: Increased LV mass with small LV cavity size, decreased ejection fraction, and impaired ventricular relaxation occurs in severe aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis murmurs decrease with maneuvers that reduce preload.
explanations.D: HCM is characterized by increased LV muscle mass and a small LV cavity. Outflow obstruction is dynamic and ejection fraction is preserved, while impaired relaxation leads to diastolic dysfunction.
explanations.E: Normal LV mass and cavity size with preserved ejection fraction and impaired LV relaxation describe restrictive cardiomyopathy.

generalExplanation: This patient with a systolic murmur along the left sternal border that decreases in intensity with maneuvers that increase left ventricular (LV) blood volume likely has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). HCM typically involves hypertrophy of the interventricular septum that can partially obstruct LV outflow and cause a murmur. Increases in LV blood volume, caused by maneuvers that increase preload (eg, passive leg elevation) or increase afterload (eg, handgrip), alleviate the LV outflow obstruction of HCM and decrease the intensity of the murmur. HCM is characterized by increased LV muscle mass and a small LV cavity. Because LV contractility is typically intact and outflow obstruction is dynamic and commonly only present with exercise, there is usually preserved ejection fraction. However, impaired relaxation of the hypertrophied LV wall typically leads to diastolic dysfunction.
educationalObjective: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) typically involves interventricular septal hypertrophy that obstructs left ventricular (LV) outflow and creates a systolic murmur that decreases in intensity with maneuvers that increase LV blood volume (eg, hand grip, passive leg elevation). HCM is characterized by increased LV muscle mass with a small LV cavity, preserved ejection fraction, and impaired LV relaxation leading to diastolic dysfunction.

stem:
A 75-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his family found him to be lethargic and confused. The patient has a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, and heart failure. Temperature is 35 C (95 F), blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. The patient is admitted to the intensive care unit and a pulmonary artery catheter is placed, which demonstrates the following readings:
- Cardiac output: high
- Central venous pressure: low
- Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure: low
- Mixed venous O2 saturation: high
- Systemic vascular resistance: low
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypotension?

explanations.A: Septic shock (usually due to bacterial infection) is characterized by low SVR due to peripheral vasodilation, low CVP and PCWP from venous pooling, high cardiac output from sympathetic compensation, and elevated SvO2 from impaired tissue extraction at high flow rates.
explanations.B: Gastrointestinal bleeding can lead to hemorrhagic shock characterized by low CVP, PCWP, and CO, with a compensatory increase in SVR.
explanations.C: Heart failure and cardiogenic shock present with high PCWP and CVP, decreased CO, and compensatory elevated SVR.
explanations.D: Mild hypothermia does not typically lead to shock, although septic shock can present with hypothermia due to hypothalamic dysregulation.
explanations.E: Myocardial infarction causing cardiogenic shock manifests as decreased cardiac output and elevated filling pressures (CVP, PCWP).
explanations.F: Acute pulmonary embolism causes obstructive shock with elevated CVP, low PCWP, decreased CO, and high SVR.

generalExplanation: This patient with severe hypotension and evidence of end-organ dysfunction is in shock. The low systemic vascular resistance (SVR) in this patient is consistent with the peripheral vasodilation that occurs in distributive shock; septic shock (usually due to bacterial infection) is the most common type. Central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) are decreased due to widespread vasodilation and reduced venous return. A compensatory increase in sympathetic drive increases cardiac contractility and heart rate resulting in increased cardiac output (CO). The high rate of blood flow through systemic capillaries prevents complete extraction of oxygen by the tissues, resulting in high mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2).
educationalObjective: Septic shock can present with either hyper- or hypothermia. The initial disturbance is peripheral vasodilation leading to decreased systemic vascular resistance, decreased central venous pressure, and decreased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. A compensatory increase in sympathetic drive causes an increase in cardiac output; the resulting high flow rates lead to incomplete oxygen extraction in the tissues, resulting in high mixed venous oxygen saturation.

stem: A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department with sudden onset of heart palpitations that started while he was at his desk at work. The patient has no known medical problems and does not use tobacco or illicit drugs. He drinks alcohol occasionally on the weekends. Initial blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg and pulse is 160/min and regular. Gentle neck massage just below the angle of the right mandible provides immediate improvement of his condition. His blood pressure is now 120/80 mm Hg and pulse is 75/min. Which of the following mechanisms is responsible for improvement of this patient's condition?

options.B: Increased sympathetic output to the sinoatrial node

explanations.A: Carotid sinus massage stretches baroreceptors and increases their firing rate rather than decreasing it.
explanations.B: Carotid sinus massage increases vagal parasympathetic output and withdraws sympathetic tone.
explanations.C: Parasympathetic activation causes vascular relaxation and reduced systemic vascular resistance.
explanations.D: Carotid sinus massage increases parasympathetic vagal efferent traffic to the AV node, slowing conduction and prolonging its refractory period, thereby terminating AV nodal reentrant tachycardia.
explanations.E: Vagal efferent fibers sparsely innervate ventricular myocardium, so ventricular refractory periods are not significantly changed.

generalExplanation: This patient's presentation with sudden onset of palpitations and rapid regular tachycardia is consistent with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), most often due to AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. Vagal maneuvers such as carotid sinus massage acutely terminate PSVT. The carotid sinus reflex has an afferent limb that arises from baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and travels via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the solitary tract nucleus. The efferent limb carries parasympathetic impulses via the vagus nerve (CN X) to the SA and AV nodes. Carotid sinus massage increases afferent firing, which increases vagal tone, slows conduction through the AV node, and prolongs the AV node refractory period, terminating the reentrant tachycardia.
educationalObjective: Carotid sinus massage leads to an increase in parasympathetic tone causing temporary inhibition of sinoatrial node activity, slowing of conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node, and prolongation of the AV node refractory period. It is a useful vagal maneuver for termination of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to pain and swelling of the right calf. He has a history of recurrent gastrointestinal hemorrhage and was discharged from the hospital 4 days ago following a prolonged admission for diverticular bleeding requiring multiple blood transfusions. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 18/min. Compression ultrasonography with Doppler reveals deep venous thrombosis in the right popliteal vein. A filter placement is planned to prevent embolization. A section of the patient's abdominal CT at the level of L2 is shown in the image below. The filter will most likely be placed in which of the following structures?

explanations.A: Structure A with its air-filled lumen and mucosal folds represents the second (descending) part of the duodenum.
explanations.B: Structure B represents the inferior vena cava (IVC), which lies anterior to the right side of the vertebral body and to the right of the abdominal aorta.
explanations.C: Structure C represents the abdominal aorta, situated to the left of the IVC.
explanations.D: Structure D represents the fourth (ascending) part of the duodenum or pancreas.
explanations.E: Structure E represents the left renal vein or left renal vessels.

generalExplanation: This patient with deep venous thrombosis (DVT) has recurrent gastrointestinal hemorrhage, creating a contraindication to anticoagulation therapy. Inferior vena cava (IVC) filter placement is planned to prevent pulmonary embolism. On abdominal CT viewed from the patient's feet, the left side of the image corresponds to the patient's right side. The IVC (labeled B) is located anterior to the right vertebral body and medial to the descending duodenum, while the abdominal aorta (labeled C) lies to the left of the midline.
educationalObjective: The inferior vena cava (IVC) courses through the abdomen and inferior thorax in a location anterior to the right half of the vertebral bodies. The renal veins join the IVC at the level of L1/L2, and the common iliac veins merge to become the IVC at the level of L5. IVC filters are placed in patients with deep venous thrombosis who have contraindications to anticoagulation therapy.

stem: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He was a restrained driver and rear-ended a slow-moving car on the highway. He complains of chest pain, abdominal pain, and difficulty breathing. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, asthma, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On arrival, his blood pressure is 98/54 mm Hg and pulse is 121/min. Thirty minutes later, he becomes unresponsive and his pulse is no longer detectable. Electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus tachycardia. Despite extensive resuscitation efforts, the patient dies. An autopsy would most likely show an injury involving which of the following areas of the thoracic aorta?

explanations.A: Traumatic aortic ruptures can affect the ascending aorta (A), but this is less common than isthmic tears.
explanations.B: The aortic arch between brachiocephalic and left common carotid branches (B) is less vulnerable than the tethered isthmus.
explanations.C: The aortic isthmus (C), located immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, is tethered by the ligamentum arteriosum and is the most common site of blunt aortic trauma.
explanations.D: The proximal descending aorta below the isthmus (D) is less commonly torn.
explanations.E: The distal thoracic descending aorta (E) is relatively mobile and less susceptible to rapid deceleration shear forces.

generalExplanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with blunt aortic injury (traumatic aortic rupture), most commonly caused by motor vehicle collisions. The mechanism involves sudden deceleration creating extreme stretching and torsional shearing forces between the relatively mobile aortic arch and the fixed descending thoracic aorta. The rupture occurs most often at the aortic isthmus, which is tethered firmly to the pulmonary trunk by the ligamentum arteriosum.
educationalObjective: Traumatic aortic rupture is most often caused by the rapid deceleration that occurs in motor vehicle collisions. The most common site of injury is the aortic isthmus, which is tethered by the ligamentum arteriosum and is relatively fixed and immobile compared to the adjacent descending aorta.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to progressive dyspnea and fatigue. Over the last week, he has not been able to lie flat due to difficulty breathing and has had to sleep in a sitting position. He had an anterior myocardial infarction 6 months ago and has not been compliant with his medication regimen since that time. Medical history is also significant for hypertension. The patient is an ex-smoker with a 30-pack-year history. He does not drink alcohol. His father died of a heart attack at age 60. Blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min and regular. Oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. He is afebrile. Auscultation reveals crackles at the lung bases, an S3 gallop, and a II/VI holosystolic murmur over the apex. The patient is admitted to the hospital, and after treatment with diuretics and vasodilators his condition improves significantly. Three days later there are no appreciable gallops or murmurs on cardiac examination. Which of the following best explains the murmur heard at the time of the initial examination?

options.B: Increased flow velocity through the aortic valve
options.E: Thickened and deformed mitral valve cusps

explanations.A: Calcification of the mitral valve annulus is usually an incidental finding with aging and does not typically produce a dynamic, reversible murmur.
explanations.B: Increased flow velocity through the aortic valve causes a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the second right intercostal space, not a dynamic apical holosystolic murmur.
explanations.C: Chordae tendineae rupture causes primary MR that does not rapidly disappear with diuretics and vasodilators and usually requires surgical repair.
explanations.D: Secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation occurs when left ventricular dilation in decompensated heart failure stretches the mitral annulus and displaces papillary muscles. Reducing preload and afterload allows the ventricle and annulus to contract, resolving the regurgitation.
explanations.E: Rheumatic valve disease causes permanent thickening and deformity that does not resolve pharmacologically.

generalExplanation: This patient's presentation with pulmonary edema, an S3 gallop, and a reversible apical holosystolic murmur is consistent with decompensated heart failure and secondary (functional) mitral valve regurgitation (MR). Decompensated heart failure increases left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), dilating the mitral valve annulus and tautly stretching the chordae tendineae. This prevents complete coaptation of intrinsically normal leaflets. Treatment with diuretics (reducing preload) and vasodilators (reducing afterload) decreases ventricular volume and restores leaflet coaptation, resolving the murmur.
educationalObjective: Decompensated heart failure is a common cause of secondary (functional) mitral valve regurgitation. Increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume causes dilation of the mitral valve annulus and restricted movement of the chordae tendineae with subsequent regurgitation. Treatment with diuretics and vasodilators can improve heart failure-induced MR.

stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up of his elevated blood pressure. The patient's medical history is significant for stable angina pectoris, for which he takes sublingual nitroglycerin as needed. He has no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower extremity swelling. His blood pressure is 154/107 mm Hg and pulse is 86/min. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The patient is started on a low dose of atenolol. Which of the following cellular changes will most likely occur as a direct effect of this medication?

options.A: Cardiomyocyte [cAMP]: Decreased | Juxtaglomerular cell [cAMP]: Decreased | Vascular smooth muscle [cAMP]: Decreased
options.B: Cardiomyocyte [cAMP]: Decreased | Juxtaglomerular cell [cAMP]: Decreased | Vascular smooth muscle [cAMP]: No significant change
options.C: Cardiomyocyte [cAMP]: Decreased | Juxtaglomerular cell [cAMP]: No significant change | Vascular smooth muscle [cAMP]: Decreased
options.D: Cardiomyocyte [cAMP]: Decreased | Juxtaglomerular cell [cAMP]: No significant change | Vascular smooth muscle [cAMP]: No significant change
options.E: Cardiomyocyte [cAMP]: No significant change | Juxtaglomerular cell [cAMP]: No significant change | Vascular smooth muscle [cAMP]: No significant change

explanations.A: Propranolol, a nonselective beta blocker, would block beta-2 receptors in vascular smooth muscle and reduce cAMP there as well, but atenolol is beta-1 selective.
explanations.B: Atenolol is a selective beta-1 adrenergic antagonist. Beta-1 receptors are Gs-coupled and found in cardiomyocytes and renal juxtaglomerular cells (reducing cAMP in both), but are not present on vascular smooth muscle.
explanations.C: Juxtaglomerular cells possess beta-1 receptors that stimulate renin release via cAMP; blocking them reduces cAMP.
explanations.D: Beta-1 blockade directly reduces cAMP in juxtaglomerular cells.
explanations.E: Beta-1 blockade significantly decreases intracellular cAMP in target tissues.

generalExplanation: Atenolol is a selective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist. Beta-1 receptors are found in cardiac tissue and on renal juxtaglomerular cells, but are not present in vascular smooth muscle (which predominantly contains alpha-1 and beta-2 receptors). The beta-1 receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor linked to Gs, which stimulates adenylyl cyclase to increase intracellular cAMP. Selective blockade of beta-1 receptors by atenolol inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP levels in cardiomyocytes and juxtaglomerular cells without directly altering cAMP levels in vascular smooth muscle.
educationalObjective: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors are found in cardiac tissue and on renal juxtaglomerular cells, but not in vascular smooth muscle. Selective blockade of the beta-1 receptor (eg, with atenolol) leads to decreased cAMP levels in cardiac and renal tissue without significantly affecting cAMP levels in vascular smooth muscle.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset right side weakness and speech difficulty. During the last 3 weeks, the patient has experienced progressive fatigue, malaise, and low-grade fevers. Despite the symptoms, she did not seek medical attention and did not take any medications. She had a dental extraction 5 weeks ago, which was uncomplicated. The patient has never previously been significantly ill or hospitalized. She works as a receptionist at a legal firm and has never traveled outside the United States. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. The patient is admitted to the hospital, but despite adequate resuscitative measures, she dies 2 hours later. Gross autopsy shows large, friable irregular masses attached to the atrial surface of a valve. Which of the following underlying conditions most likely predisposed this patient to developing these cardiac changes?

explanations.A: Atrial septal defects create low-velocity shunt flow between low-pressure chambers and rarely predispose to infective endocarditis.
explanations.B: Coronary artery disease can cause ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction but does not classically predispose to native valve endocarditis in young patients.
explanations.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy rarely causes endocarditis unless significant subaortic turbulent jets damage the endothelium.
explanations.D: Mitral annular calcification is typically seen in patients over 60 years old and is not a common predisposing factor for endocarditis in a young adult.
explanations.E: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) with coexistent mitral regurgitation is the most common predisposing condition for native valve infective endocarditis in developed countries.

generalExplanation: This patient had subacute infective endocarditis (IE) complicated by an embolic stroke from large, friable vegetations on the mitral valve. In developed nations, mitral valve prolapse (MVP), particularly with regurgitation, is the most common underlying valvular pathology predisposing to IE. Turbulent flow creates microscopic endothelial injury, leading to sterile platelet-fibrin deposition that becomes colonized during transient bacteremia (such as following dental procedures). While rheumatic heart disease remains a frequent cause in developing countries, MVP has surpassed it in developed nations.
educationalObjective: Mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation is the most common predisposing condition for native valve infective endocarditis (IE) in developed nations. Rheumatic heart disease remains a frequent cause of IE in developing nations.
